notes:
I've put together notes for all 23 verses (vv. 24–46). There were limits on what I could check, and they affect sections 2 and 3:

- **How I read the sources:** I opened Enduring Word through search excerpts and read a Precept Austin page, but that page cut off before v. 24. The Pulpit Commentary page on StudyLight wouldn't load, so I only have the parts of it quoted on BibleHub. The rest comes from search excerpts of BibleHub and StudyLight.
- **Section 2 (where Protestant traditions differ):** I didn't find any source on these verses saying one tradition disagrees with another. The only tradition label a source gave me is "Baptist" for John Gill (StudyLight). I've left other commentators unlabelled rather than assign traditions from memory.
- **Section 3 (other views):** The only modern-scholarship voice I found is the Cambridge Bible, plus one NET Bible note quoted on Precept Austin. I found nothing from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org, and nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching.

---

**v. 24**
- Guzik: the best parts of the second ram were put together with the bread, cake and wafer and first waved before God in an act of presentation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-29/
- Matthew Henry: the pieces were first put into the hands of Aaron to be waved to and fro, in token of their being offered to God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/29-37.html
- Biblical Illustrator: this rite was called "the filling of the hands." It was so central that "to fill the hand" came to mean consecrating someone as a priest. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/exodus-29.html

**v. 25**
- Guzik: after the waving, these portions were burnt on the altar as an act of complete devotion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-29/
- Henry: the altar was to devour God's part of the sacrifice. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/29-37.html
- Preacher's Homiletical: burning these pieces showed that the priest's office was about winning God's favour for others. The gifts also stood for humility and devotion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/exodus-29.html

**v. 26**
- Ellicott: normally the breast of a wave offering went to the officiating priest. Here Moses was officiating, so it was given to him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-29.html
- Henry: Moses, acting as God's agent, now did the priest's work, and therefore that which was the priest's part of the sacrifice was here ordered to be his. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_029.cfm

**vv. 27–28**
- Ellicott: from then on, the breast and right shoulder from consecration offerings went to the officiating priest. "Heaving" was one upward lift; "waving" was a repeated back-and-forth movement. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-29.html
- Coffman: waving toward the altar showed the gift was given to God, and waving back showed God returning it as the priests' food. He adds that "forever" here does not mean "eternity." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/29-28.html
- Gill (Baptist): the priests got the shoulder because Aaron carried Israel's names on his shoulders, and the breast because he carried them on his heart. The statute lasted as long as Aaron's priesthood, until the Messiah came. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/29-28.htm
- Clarke, citing Ainsworth: the breast and shoulder taught the priests to give themselves to God's service with all their heart and all their strength. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/29-27.html
- Bridgeway: giving the priests these parts showed God's acceptance and fellowship, and waving them first admitted that everything belonged to Him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/29-18.html

**v. 29**
- Ellicott: this verse implies that each later high priest was to be anointed, and Jewish tradition says that was the practice. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-29.html
- Guzik: future descendants of Aaron would be consecrated in the same way. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-29/

**v. 30**
- Henry: the successor wore the garments seven days as a sign of a slow, deliberate entry into office, so that one sabbath might pass over him in his consecration. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_029.cfm

**vv. 31–33**
- Guzik: for seven days the priests lived at the tabernacle and ate the ram and bread. The meal came after the washing, clothing and blood, and it pictures their ongoing relationship with God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-29/
- Constable: a covenant meal always went with this kind of arrangement (compare Exodus 24:11), and that is what the shared ram means. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/29-37.html
- Calvin: holy food could not be eaten at home, so that it stayed distinct from ordinary meals and taught reverence. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/29-28.html
- On v. 33's "no outsider", Guzik says believers today may still share this priestly relationship, based on 1 Peter 2:5 and 2:9. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-29/
- Biblical Illustrator: it links the ordination meal to the Last Supper, saying the apostles were consecrated by a similar "filling of the hands" when Jesus put bread in their hands. It also says early Greek ordination services put part of the consecrated elements into the new priest's hands. This is a Protestant commentary describing Eastern practice, not an Orthodox source. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/exodus-29.html

**v. 34**
- Chuck Smith: anything not eaten was burned, reserved for God's servants alone. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/29-37.html

**v. 35**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: repeating the rites every day for seven days, with a Sabbath in between, gave time for calm and devout reflection. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Exd/Exd_029.cfm
- Guzik: the ceremony wasn't quick or easy. It took time and constant awareness of sacrifice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-29/

**v. 36**
- Pulpit: the altar had been defiled by the sin of the men serving at it, so it also needed cleansing with the sin offering's blood. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/exodus-29.html
- Henry: the daily sin offerings could not make the comers thereunto perfect, for then they would have ceased to be offered, as the apostle argues, Heb. 10:1, 2. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_029.cfm

**v. 37** (the most debated verse)
- Pulpit, following Kalisch: "most holy" is literally "holiness of holinesses". The last clause should read "must be holy", meaning nothing unholy may touch the altar. Ellicott agrees: the future tense works as a command, as in the Ten Commandments. https://biblehub.com/exodus/29-37.htm
- Clarke: Jesus refers to this in Matthew 23:19. Whatever was laid on the altar became the Lord's property. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/29-37.html
- Poole and Gill: this applies to gifts that belonged on the altar, not to everything, because Haggai 2:12 shows unclean things are not made holy by touching. Gill also treats the altar as a picture of Christ, who makes believers' prayer and praise acceptable. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/29-37.htm
- Chuck Smith applies it personally: if you lay your life on the altar, it is God's and not yours to take back. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/exodus-29.html
- Modern scholarship (Cambridge Bible): it sees here a survival of primitive ideas of 'holiness.' Holiness spreads by contact, and a careless person who touched holy things could forfeit even his life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/29-37.htm

**vv. 38–39**
- Ellicott/Pulpit: the lambs partly made amends for the nation's daily sins. Mainly they were a sign that Israel renewed its dedication to God every day. https://biblehub.com/exodus/29-38.htm
- Calvin: the lambs reminded Israel of its guilt from morning to evening, so that it might learn to fly to God's mercy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/29-38.html
- Matthew Henry: the daily lamb pictures Christ's continual intercession and calls believers to morning and evening prayer and praise. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/29-38.html
- Modern scholarship (Cambridge Bible): vv. 38–42 interrupt the flow from v. 37 to v. 43, so they were probably brought in from Numbers 28 by a later hand. It adds that before the exile only the morning offering was a burnt offering; the evening one was a grain offering. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/29-38.htm

**v. 40**
- Barnes: the lamb showed that the people's life belonged to God; the flour showed their work was His due. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/29-41.html
- Ellicott: Scripture doesn't say how the drink offering was disposed of. Josephus says it was poured on the altar; others say part went to the priests, which Ellicott thinks more likely. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/29-38.htm

**v. 41**
- Guzik: these fully burned offerings pleased God, who is honoured by our complete surrender. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-29/

**v. 42**
- Pulpit: this verse settles the meaning of the phrase: it is the "tabernacle of meeting", where God meets His people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/29-42.htm
- Ellicott: the shift from "you" (plural) to "you" (singular) shows God would speak through the high priest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/29-38.htm
- Guzik: apart from captivity and national apostasy, these offerings continued until New Testament times. God wanted to meet and speak with His people, not just have an efficient workforce. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-29/

**v. 43**
- Keil & Delitzsch: what is "sanctified" here is Israel as a nation, not the altar as most commentators assume. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/29-45.htm
- Barnes: "tabernacle" is the wrong word to supply; it means the place where God meets the assembly. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/29-45.html
- NET note: God's presence sanctifies, which points to Exodus 40:34. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-29-commentary
- Guzik: God's presence truly made the place holy. What the priests did removed the barriers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-29/

**v. 44**
- Matthew Henry: What is sanctified to the glory of God shall be sanctified by his glory. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_029.cfm
- Guzik (via Precept Austin): Leviticus 9:23–24 records the result, when God's glory appeared to all the people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-29-commentary

**v. 45**
- Pulpit: this mainly means the Shechinah (God's visible presence) in the holy of holies, but God would also be with His people in many other ways. https://biblehub.com/exodus/29-45.htm
- Poole: God dwells there by special grace, since His essence already fills every place. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/29-45.htm
- Barnes: the goal was for the whole nation to live in God's presence as "a kingdom of priests." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/29-45.htm
- Clarke: this is the great charter of the people of God in both Testaments. Under the New Covenant, God also dwells in believers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/29-45.html

**v. 46**
- Calvin: God was not just a one-time deliverer; He would show in practice that He lives among them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/29-46.html
- Gill: God's dwelling among them was a far greater mercy than the land itself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/29-46.html
- Clarke: God dwells among people so they may know Him, and they must keep knowing and obeying Him for Him to stay. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/29-46.html
- Pulpit: No other God could deliver after this sort. No other God could be so long-suffering to a "stiff-necked people." https://biblehub.com/exodus/29-46.htm
